topics.title: What is SANS?
topics.text: SANS is a set of eye and neuro-ocular changes linked to long spaceflights. It can change the shape of the eyeball and the optic nerve. Not everyone has symptoms. Following vision and eye images over time helps detect changes that need an assessment.
topics.source: NASA - Risk of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)

topics.title: Why do astronauts lose bone?
topics.text: In microgravity bones carry less load and can lose mineral density. This raises the risk of fragility, especially on long missions. Resistance exercise and other countermeasures reduce the loss but do not remove every risk. The assessment depends on each astronaut's history.
topics.source: NASA Human Research Program - musculoskeletal risks

topics.title: What is silent jugular thrombosis?
topics.text: In microgravity body fluids shift and the venous flow in the neck can change. Jugular vein thrombosis has been described in astronauts, even without clear symptoms. Ultrasound can provide information, but an app alert is not a diagnosis.
topics.source: NASA OCHMO - Venous thrombosis in spaceflight

topics.title: Why does CO2 matter?
topics.text: The cabin is a closed environment and carbon dioxide must be controlled all the time. High levels can be linked to headache and other effects on wellbeing or performance. With symptoms, check the environmental readings and follow mission procedures, without automatically blaming CO2.
topics.source: NASA OCHMO - Carbon dioxide technical brief

topics.title: What is the radiation dose?
topics.text: Space radiation includes particles from the Sun and from deep space. The cumulative dose is one of the variables used to assess risk, but it is not enough on its own: the type of exposure and its duration also matter. Protective measures depend on the mission and on agency protocols.
topics.source: NASA - Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight

topics.title: Do medicines expire earlier in space?
topics.text: Some medicines studied after staying on the ISS showed stability problems. Those results do not let us set a new expiry date for every drug: formulation, packaging and storage all matter. SOSpesIA separates the label expiry date from a stability alert that has not been validated.
topics.source: Du et al. (2011), Evaluation of Physical and Chemical Changes in Pharmaceuticals Flown on Space Missions

topics.title: Why does Earth take so long to answer?
topics.text: Communication with a distant spacecraft is not instant: radio signals travel at the speed of light. On missions to Mars the wait can be several minutes each way, and weeks with no link during solar conjunction. That is why some urgent measures must be planned in onboard protocols and not depend on an immediate answer from Earth.
topics.source: JPL approximate planetary positions (team link table)

topics.title: What is adaptive monitoring?
topics.text: It means reading a measurement against the person's usual pattern and the mission conditions, and measuring more only when something justifies it. A change from the baseline can trigger a check, but does not prove a disease on its own. It is an approach proposed by SOSpesIA, not a validated clinical function.
topics.source: SOSpesIA team proposal (internal source, not clinical evidence)

topics.title: What is the IMM?
topics.text: The Integrated Medical Model (IMM) is a NASA modelling tool used to study medical risks of space missions. It helps explore scenarios and resource needs, but its estimates are not individual diagnoses.

topics.title: What is the authority dial?
topics.text: It is a SOSpesIA visual that compares how long Earth needs to answer with how urgent an incident is (A = Earth response time / time available). It explains when a crew may need to apply a pre-approved protocol without waiting for Earth. It does not replace medical judgement or authorise any intervention by itself.
